title: The Second Bell
subject: rla
passage:
Elena arrived at the auditorium forty minutes before the student orchestra was due to perform. She placed spare clothespins on the music stands, taped the extension cords along the wall, and checked the order of the pieces against the printed program. Marcus, the trumpet player, watched her from the front row.

"You know we're indoors, right?" he said, holding up one of the clothespins. "The music isn't going to blow away."

Elena smiled and put the clothespin back. "Probably not today."

Marcus had teased her before about preparing for problems that had not happened. Elena kept a box labeled JUST IN CASE under her chair at rehearsals. It held pencils, tape, spare strings, a small flashlight, and a copy of every student's emergency contact number. Most rehearsals ended without anyone opening it.

Ten minutes before the concert, the lights flickered and went out. The stage went dark, and the projector that displayed translations of the songs disappeared with them. A maintenance worker hurried toward the electrical room and said he could not promise how quickly power would return.

The orchestra director looked at the rows of arriving families. "We can delay," she said, "but I don't know for how long."

Elena opened the JUST IN CASE box and handed out the small flashlights. Then she pointed to the first piece on the program, a short work that did not require piano or projected text. The director moved the orchestra to the front edge of the stage, where light from the lobby reached them, and asked the audience to wait while the musicians settled.

They began the acoustic piece without amplification. Halfway through it, the ceiling lights returned. The projector took another few minutes to restart, so the director changed the order and placed a second acoustic piece next. By the third selection, the program was back on its original plan.

After the concert, Marcus found Elena gathering the flashlights. "I still think the clothespins were unnecessary," he said.

"Today," Elena replied.

A month later, the orchestra prepared for an outdoor afternoon concert. Elena arrived to find a bag of wooden clothespins on every row of stands. Marcus was at the back of the stage, checking the weather forecast on his phone.

While the musicians packed up after the first concert, the director thanked Elena for having materials ready but also reminded the group that preparation was not the same as predicting every problem. "We cannot carry a solution for everything," she said. "But we can notice which small preparations give us more choices when plans change." Marcus glanced at the box without answering.

"Wind after three," he called. "I brought extras." Elena clipped her music to the stand and said nothing, but Marcus noticed her smile.

questions.prompt: Which event happens immediately after the power goes out?
questions.explanation: The maintenance worker responds immediately after the outage.
questions.rule: Track the event directly around the target moment.

options.text: Marcus brings clothespins to the outdoor concert
options.whyWrong: “Marcus brings clothespins to the outdoor concert” happens later, not at the point in the sequence the question asks about.

options.text: A maintenance worker goes toward the electrical room and cannot promise a quick repair
The orchestra finishes the third selection
options.whyWrong: “The orchestra finishes the third selection” happens later, not at the point in the sequence the question asks about.

options.text: Elena arrives at the auditorium
options.whyWrong: “Elena arrives at the auditorium” happens earlier, not at the point in the sequence the question asks about.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: Ten minutes before the concert, the lights flickered and went out.

questions.prompt: How does the power outage affect the concert?
questions.explanation: The outage removes lighting/projected text, so the group starts with acoustic pieces and changes the order.
questions.rule: State how the event changes later actions.

options.text: It causes the audience to leave permanently
options.whyWrong: “It causes the audience to leave permanently” connects details that the passage does not present as meaningfully related.

options.text: It forces the orchestra to change how and in what order it performs the opening pieces
It proves the orchestra did not rehearse
options.whyWrong: “It proves the orchestra did not rehearse” connects details that the passage does not present as meaningfully related.

options.text: It has no effect on the program
options.whyWrong: “It has no effect on the program” describes order, but the question asks how one event affects another.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: Elena opened the JUST IN CASE box ... pointed to the first piece ... did not require piano or projected text.

questions.prompt: How is Marcus different at the outdoor concert from the beginning of the story?
questions.explanation: His later actions show that he has adopted the kind of advance preparation he had teased Elena about.
questions.rule: Compare attitude and behavior at two points in the story.

options.text: He still believes all preparation is pointless
options.whyWrong: “He still believes all preparation is pointless” assigns the two subjects’ features to the wrong sides of the comparison.

options.text: He stops playing music entirely
options.whyWrong: “He stops playing music entirely” focuses on a minor difference that does not answer the comparison being asked.

options.text: He now prepares for wind by checking the forecast and bringing clothespins
He becomes the orchestra director
options.whyWrong: “He becomes the orchestra director” treats the subjects as similar in a way the text does not support.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: A month later ... a bag of wooden clothespins ... Marcus ... checking the weather forecast ... "I brought extras."

questions.prompt: What can the reader most reasonably infer about Elena's idea of preparation?
questions.explanation: Her JUST IN CASE box is rarely used, yet she continues preparing and the supplies help during the outage.
questions.rule: Infer the principle that explains repeated behavior, not an extreme motive.

options.text: She believes small preparations can be worthwhile even when most of them are not needed on a given day
She believes preparation is useful only when a problem is guaranteed
options.whyWrong: “She believes preparation is useful only when a problem is guaranteed” conflicts with a specific detail in the passage.

options.text: She expects every concert to fail
options.whyWrong: “She expects every concert to fail” could be possible, but the passage does not provide enough evidence to support that conclusion.

options.text: She prepares mainly to impress Marcus
options.whyWrong: “She prepares mainly to impress Marcus” assigns a motive that the text never gives. Use only motives supported by actions or wording.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: Elena arrived ... spare clothespins ... extension cords ... checked the order ... JUST IN CASE box.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion about Marcus is best supported by the ending?
questions.explanation: At the outdoor concert he checks the forecast and supplies clothespins himself, showing changed behavior.
questions.rule: Use the ending together with his earlier attitude.

options.text: He has completely stopped joking with Elena
options.whyWrong: “He has completely stopped joking with Elena” predicts an outcome the passage does not establish.

options.text: He dislikes outdoor performances
options.whyWrong: “He dislikes outdoor performances” relies too heavily on one detail instead of combining the relevant clues.

options.text: He now believes every possible item must be carried to every concert
options.whyWrong: “He now believes every possible item must be carried to every concert” goes beyond the scope of the text. The evidence supports a narrower claim.

options.text: The outage experience has influenced him to take advance preparation more seriously

questions.evidenceExcerpt: A month later ... a bag of wooden clothespins ... Marcus ... checking the weather forecast ... "I brought extras."

questions.prompt: What causes the director to move the first performance toward the front edge of the stage?
questions.explanation: The lack of power and available lobby light explain the location change.
questions.rule: Find the mechanism connecting the problem to the response.

options.text: The power outage leaves the stage dark, while lobby light is still available
Marcus asks for a different seat
options.whyWrong: “Marcus asks for a different seat” gives chronology without explaining the relationship the question asks about.

options.text: The audience requests clothespins
options.whyWrong: “The audience requests clothespins” shows that two things occurred together, but that alone does not establish causation.

options.text: The weather forecast predicts wind next month
options.whyWrong: “The weather forecast predicts wind next month” is an effect or result, not the cause the question asks for.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: Elena opened the JUST IN CASE box ... pointed to the first piece ... did not require piano or projected text.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?
questions.explanation: The story develops this idea through Elena's habits, the outage, and Marcus's changed behavior.
questions.rule: Theme explains what the events suggest, not just what happened.

options.text: Power outages always improve concerts
options.whyWrong: “Power outages always improve concerts” turns a limited pattern into a rule that is broader than the evidence supports.

options.text: Every musician should carry the same emergency box
options.whyWrong: “Every musician should carry the same emergency box” states a moral that the story’s events do not clearly develop.

options.text: Careful preparation can seem excessive until an unexpected problem reveals its value
Elena brings flashlights to a concert and Marcus later brings clothespins
options.whyWrong: “Elena brings flashlights to a concert and Marcus later brings clothes…” retells events instead of expressing the theme or general message.

questions.evidenceExcerpt: Preparation for unlikely problems can become valuable, and experience can change how people judge that preparation.
